after: ## What counts as a personal investigation
alt: Five linked stages of a fieldwork enquiry, from planning to conclusions, with their specification numbers. A bar to scale shows 15 of Unit 5's 60 marks assess the student's own investigation. Below, acceptable alternatives to practical fieldwork and what is not acceptable.
caption: Five stages of enquiry; 15 of the 60 marks are on your own investigation.

alt: Three linked boxes using the invented Marton example: the aim (how footfall changes with distance from the centre), the hypothesis (footfall decreases with distance from the main square) and its justification in bid-rent theory. A note explains when to use a research question instead.
caption: Aim, then a testable hypothesis, justified by a theory you have studied.

alt: A three-by-three grid of likelihood against severity, with four numbered hazards placed on it: traffic (medium, high), fast-flowing river water (low to medium, high), hot weather (medium, medium) and lone working (low, high). A table gives the control measure for each.
caption: Judge each hazard's likelihood and severity, then set a control measure.

alt: A bar to scale divides 80 questionnaires by the area's age shares: 28% aged 18-34 gives 22 people, 47% aged 35-64 gives 38, and 25% aged 65 and over gives 20. Eighty circles show the split, which checks to 80. A note explains why stratifying by age matters.
caption: Multiply the sample size by each group's share, round, then check the total.

alt: A three-by-three grid of schematic plan views: random, systematic and stratified sampling, each applied at points, along line transects and within area quadrats. In the stratified column a shaded zone receives samples in proportion to its size.
caption: Any of the three methods can be applied at points, along lines or within areas.

alt: Four cards define accuracy (close to the true value), precision (fineness of scale), reliability (similar results if repeated) and validity (measuring what the hypothesis is about). An example: one footfall count on a rainy Monday may be accurate for that moment but is neither reliable nor valid as typical footfall.
caption: Accurate is not the same as reliable, and neither guarantees validity.

alt: Table matching data to presentation and analysis techniques: proportional circles for footfall at sites, scatter graph and Spearman's rank for footfall against distance, cross-section for channel shape, annotated photographs for land use, chi-square for categories, central tendency and dispersion for comparing sites, and coding for interviews.
caption: Choose each technique to fit the data, and justify the choice.

after: ## Worked example: a familiar fieldwork answer
alt: Six steps of a model familiar fieldwork answer on sampling: state the method, give a strength linked to the hypothesis, limitations with evidence, reliability, a specific improvement and an overall judgement.
caption: Method, strength, limitation, reliability, improvement, judgement.
